lesson.title: The Whole Story: Assembling the Complete Response
lesson.summary: The complete response is the full solution of a first-order circuit, built by adding the natural response (the decaying transient set by initial conditions) to the forced response (the steady value set by the source), and it describes circuit behavior at every instant in time, not just at the beginning or the end.
lesson.body:
Natural response and forced response each tell half a story, and neither one by itself describes what a real circuit does after a switch flips. The natural response describes how stored energy in a capacitor or inductor would behave with no source connected at all, decaying exponentially toward zero at a rate set by the time constant. The forced response describes where the circuit is ultimately headed because of the source, ignoring how it got there. Add the two together, term for term, and you get the complete response: a single expression valid at every moment from the instant of switching all the way out to steady state.

The general template for a first-order complete response is x(t) = x_forced + [x(0) - x_forced] x e^(-t/tau), where x(0) is the initial condition, x_forced is the forced response (equal to x(infinity) for a step input), and tau is the time constant. Notice that at t = 0 the exponential term equals 1, so the formula correctly returns x(0); and as t grows large the exponential term vanishes, so the formula correctly settles to x_forced. Everything covered so far, natural response, forced response, and final conditions, exists specifically to supply the three numbers this one formula needs.

Return to the RL circuit from the forced response discussion: a 15 V source drives R1 = 5 ohms in series with inductor L, with R2 = 10 ohms across the inductor. The forced current was found to be i_forced = 3 A. Suppose the inductor starts with zero current, i(0) = 0 A, and L = 2 H. The time constant for the natural response is tau = L / R_th, where R_th is the resistance seen by the inductor with the source zeroed out, which is R1 in parallel with R2: R_th = (5 x 10)/(5 + 10) = 50/15 = 3.333 ohms. So tau = 2 H / 3.333 ohms = 0.6 s.

Plugging into the template: i(t) = 3 + (0 - 3)e^(-t/0.6) = 3 - 3e^(-t/0.6) amps. At t = 0.6 s, exactly one time constant in, i = 3 - 3e^-1 = 3 - 3(0.3679) = 3 - 1.104 = 1.896 A. At t = 1.8 s, three time constants in, i = 3 - 3e^-3 = 3 - 3(0.0498) = 3 - 0.149 = 2.851 A, clearly converging on the forced value of 3 A. Every point along this curve is the complete response: correct at the start, correct at the finish, and correct everywhere in between.

It is worth naming the two terms in the final expression explicitly, because exams and datasheets both expect you to recognize them on sight. The constant 3 A is the forced response, unchanged from the earlier calculation and independent of the initial condition entirely. The decaying piece, -3e^(-t/0.6), is the natural response, and its coefficient of -3 came directly from the mismatch between the initial condition (0 A) and the forced response (3 A); had the inductor started with some nonzero current instead, only that coefficient would change, not the exponential shape or the time constant.

This assembled formula is exactly what circuit engineers mean by "solving" a first-order transient circuit, and it is also exactly what the step response, covered next, formalizes as a standard procedure specifically for step-function sources like the one used in this example.
